verdict.rationale: The claim has two parts and the word-level pattern lands them very differently. The no-date-setting part is decisive across multiple Bible authors. Matthew 24:36 and Mark 13:32 use the universal negative pronoun 'no one' (oudeis) with the perfect tense (a completed action whose result still stands) 'knows' (oiden) of the day (hemera) and hour (hora). Mark stacks the negatives 'neither ... nor' (oude ... oude) to deny even the Son. Acts 1:7 says 'it is not yours to know times or seasons which the Father has fixed by his own authority' (ouch hymon estin gnonai chronous e kairous hous ho pater etheto en te idia exousia), removing the times and seasons from the disciples' competence. Paul reuses the same 'time' (chronos) and 'season' (kairos) pair in 1 Thessalonians 5:1 and adds the thief comparison of 1 Thessalonians 5:2. Watchfulness is commanded with present imperatives (ongoing commands) 'keep watching' (gregoreite) in Matthew 24:42, 'watch and stay alert' (blepete agrupneite) in Mark 13:33, and 'be ready' (ginesthe hetoimoi) in Matthew 24:44. The any-moment imminence emphasis is real but more synthetic. The thief comparison and watch-commands plus Philippians 4:5 'near' (engys), James 5:8 'has drawn near' (engiken), and Revelation 22:20 'I come swiftly' (erchomai tachy) support nearness and readiness, while 2 Thessalonians 2:1-3 inserts an ordered 'falling away' (apostasia) and revealing of the 'man of lawlessness' (anthropos tes anomias) before the day comes, so a strict any-moment expectation is in tension with at least one sequence statement in the canon (the whole Bible).

scripture.force: Matthew 24:36 opens with 'but concerning that day and hour' (peri de tes hemeras ekeines kai horas) and then negates knowledge with 'no one knows' (oudeis oiden). The pronoun 'no one' (oudeis) is a universal negative, so the perfect tense (a completed action whose result still stands) 'knows' (oiden, tagged in MorphGNT as perfect active indicative third singular, the standard stative perfect meaning to know) is denied to every named party, the angels of heaven and even the Son, leaving 'except the Father alone' (ei me ho pater monos). The day (hemera) and hour (hora) are explicitly named as the unknown items, which fixes the non-knowledge part of the proposition at the word level.

The present active imperative 'keep watching' (gregoreite, an ongoing command) commands continuous watchfulness, and the 'because' (hoti) clause grounds it in 'you do not know on what day your Lord is coming' (ouk oidate poia hemera ho kyrios hymon erchetai). The question-word 'what kind of day' (poia hemera) makes the unknown a specific calendar item, and the present-tense 'is coming' (erchetai, an ongoing or imminent action) keeps the coming in view as something that can break in at any time. The watchfulness command is presented as the direct response to not knowing the day.

The comparison likens the coming to a thief: 'if the master of the house had known in what watch the thief was coming, he would have stayed awake' (ei edei ho oikodespotes poia phylake ho kleptes erchetai, egregoresen an). The pluperfect 'had known' (edei) in a contrary-to-fact 'if-then' clause states that the householder did not know the watch, and the main clause 'he would have stayed awake' (egregoresen an) makes watchfulness contingent on that ignorance. The 'thief' (kleptes) image encodes unpredictability of timing.

The conclusion 'be ready' (ginesthe hetoimoi) uses the predicate adjective 'ready' (hetoimos, the word completing a 'be Y' statement) of readiness and is grounded by 'because at an hour you do not expect the Son of Man is coming' (hoti he ou dokeite hora ho huios tou anthropou erchetai). The verb 'expect, think' (dokeo) marks the hour as one the hearers do not expect, and the present-tense 'is coming' (erchetai) again presents the coming as possible at an unanticipated hour. Readiness is commanded precisely because the hour (hora) is not predictable.

Jesus answers the disciples' question about the kingdom's restoration with 'it is not yours to know times or seasons which the Father has fixed by his own authority' (ouch hymon estin gnonai chronous e kairous hous ho pater etheto en te idia exousia). The negated possessive 'not yours' (ouch hymon) plus the aorist infinitive (a completed-action verbal noun) 'to know' (gnonai) removes the knowing of times and seasons from the disciples' province, and the relative clause assigns those 'times' (chronoi) and 'seasons' (kairoi) to the Father's own authority. This is the direct word-level ground for forbidding speculation or date-setting about the timing.

Paul writes 'but concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need to have anything written to you' (peri de ton chronon kai ton kairon, adelphoi, ou chreian echete hymin graphesthai). The same 'time' (chronos) and 'season' (kairos) pair as Acts 1:7 appears, and Paul says no calendar instruction needs to be written, which presupposes that fixing the time is not the church's task. The word-level overlap with Acts ties the two passages on the question of timing.

Paul states 'for you yourselves know precisely that the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night' (autoi gar akribos oidate hoti hemera kyriou hos kleptes en nykti houtos erchetai). What they know precisely ('precisely' = akribos) is not the date but the manner, that the day (hemera) of the Lord comes like a thief (kleptes) in the night. The 'thief in the night' (kleptes en nykti) comparison reuses the Matthew 24:43 image and encodes unannounced arrival, supporting imminence (nearness ready to break in) without a knowable date.

Mark's parallel is fuller: 'but concerning that day or the hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, but only the Father' (peri de tes hemeras ekeines e tes horas oudeis oiden, oude hoi angeloi en ourano oude ho huios, ei me ho pater). The 'no one' (oudeis) plus the stacked 'neither ... nor' (oude ... oude) exhausts the candidates and ascribes knowledge only to the Father. This is the strongest single statement of the non-knowledge part in the canon (the whole Bible).

The application 'watch, stay alert' (blepete, agrupneite) pairs two present imperatives (ongoing commands) of vigilance, grounded by 'for you do not know when the time is' (ouk oidate gar pote ho kairos estin). The question-word 'when' (pote) plus the negated 'you know' (oidate) states that the time (kairos) is unknown, and 'watch' (blepo) plus 'stay alert' (agrupneo, a rare verb, only four occurrences in the Greek New Testament, three of them with end-times or prayer-alertness force) command continuous alertness as the response. This matches the Matthew 24:42 'keep watching' (gregoreite) pattern with a second vigilance verb.

Paul writes 'the Lord is near' (ho kyrios engys), with the adverb 'near' (engys). Whether the nearness is temporal (return soon) or spatial (presence near), the temporal reading is well attested for 'near' (engys) when paired with day-or-coming language, and the immediate ethical command 'let your gentleness be known' (epieikes hymon gnostheto) makes nearness function as a readiness motive. Supports the imminence (nearness) part without specifying calendar timing.

James writes 'the coming of the Lord has drawn near' (he parousia tou kyriou engiken). The perfect indicative 'has drawn near' (engiken, a completed action whose result still stands) of 'draw near' (engizo) is stative, has drawn near and still stands near, and is the same verb form used in Matthew 3:2 and 4:17 for the kingdom drawing near. The perfect (a completed action whose result still stands) carries a sense of nearness without specifying a date, supporting imminence (nearness) and forbidding the calendar by remaining indefinite.

The risen Christ says 'yes, I am coming swiftly' (nai, erchomai tachy). The present-tense 'I come' (erchomai) with the adverb 'swiftly, soon' (tachy) asserts an arrival that is swift and unspecified. 'Swiftly' (tachy) is a sparse word (ten New Testament occurrences) and its concentration in Revelation (six of ten) is a small canon-distinctive cluster that ties the closing of the canon (the whole Bible) to the unannounced-arrival pattern. No date is implied.

complicating_texts.resolution: Just before the date-denial Jesus says 'when you see all these things, know that it is near' (hotan idete panta tauta, ginoskete hoti engys estin), you can know it is near (engys) when you see all these things. This might look like permission to read signs and infer a date. The word-level answer is that 'know ... near' (ginoskete ... engys) establishes recognizable nearness of the season, not the day (hemera) or hour (hora), while verse 36 immediately denies 'no one knows' (oudeis oiden) of the precise day (hemera) and hour (hora). The two statements operate at different granularities, general nearness versus exact timing, so they cohere rather than conflict and the date-setting ban stands.

Paul tells the believers 'but you, brothers, are not in darkness, that the day should overtake you like a thief' (hymeis de, adelphoi, ouk este en skotei, hina he hemera hymas hos kleptes katalabe), that the day (hemera) should not overtake them like a thief (kleptes). This could be read as exempting believers from the thief-like unpredictability. The word-level force is that the contrast is between moral readiness (children of light) and being caught unprepared, not between knowing and not knowing the date. The thief (kleptes) comparison of verse 2 is not retracted, the unpredictability of timing remains, and watchfulness rather than calendar knowledge is the prescribed posture.

The clause 'nor the Son' (oude ho huios), that not even the Son knows, raises a tension about Christ's nature that some treat as undermining the proposition's coherence. For this word-level verdict the clause actually strengthens the non-knowledge part, since the universal negation extends through the highest created and even the Son's own knowledge to reserve the day (hemera) for the Father alone (pater). The proposition is about whether the day is humanly knowable and forbidden to set, and 'nor the Son' (oude ho huios) makes the denial maximal, so it is supportive rather than complicating for the timing claim.

Paul writes 'now we ask you, brothers, concerning the coming of our Lord ... that you not be quickly shaken ... as if the day of the Lord has come' (erotomen de hymas, adelphoi, hyper tes parousias tou kyriou ... eis to me tacheos saleuthenai hymas ... hos hoti enesteken he hemera tou kyriou), and then explicitly orders the sequence 'unless the falling away comes first and the man of lawlessness is revealed' (hoti ean me elthe he apostasia proton kai apokalyphthe ho anthropos tes anomias). The adverb 'first' (proton) and the aorist subjunctives (completed-action conditional verbs) place a 'falling away' (apostasia) and the revealing of the 'man of lawlessness' (anthropos tes anomias) before the day (hemera). At the word level this complicates the strict any-moment part of the proposition (an unconditional any-moment expectation) but does NOT complicate the no-date-setting part, since the sequence does not yield a date, and even Paul's framing turns on 'being shaken' (saleuthenai, do not be shaken) rather than calculation. The no-date-setting verdict is robust. The any-moment phrasing of the imminence part is the contested element, and that contest is named honestly in the competing_lens_verdicts below.

variant_units_examined.note: Some manuscript witnesses omit 'nor the Son' (oude ho huios) in Matthew 24:36, harmonizing toward a shorter reading, while the Mark 13:32 parallel retains it unambiguously. The non-knowledge verdict holds with or without the clause in Matthew because 'no one knows' (oudeis oiden) already denies knowledge universally and Mark carries the fuller form.

Witnesses differ on whether 'and pray' (kai proseuchesthe) follows 'watch, stay alert' (blepete agrupneite). The lexical-graph tokens for Mark 13:33 include G4336 (proseuchomai, 'to pray'), consistent with the longer reading, but the watchfulness-plus-unknown-time verdict rests on 'watch, stay alert' (blepete, agrupneite) and 'you do not know when' (ouk oidate pote) and is unaffected either way.

variants.note: All anchor verses are in the Gospels, Acts, 1 Thessalonians, Philippians, James, and Revelation, which are New Testament books outside 3 John where the ECM (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) is not yet published. Readings taken from the standard critical editions in shadow mode.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the present imperatives (ongoing commands) 'keep watching' (gregoreite) and 'watch, stay alert' (blepete agrupneite) plus the thief (kleptes) comparison and 'I come swiftly' (erchomai tachy) as teaching constant readiness for an any-moment return without prior signs that affect the believer. The word-level denial of a known day (hemera) or hour (hora) supports the no-date-setting clause directly, and Philippians 4:5 'near' (engys) plus James 5:8 'has drawn near' (engiken) are read as actual temporal nearness.

Reads 2 Thessalonians 2:1-3 with the ordering adverb 'first' (proton) and the aorist subjunctives (completed-action conditional verbs) as inserting a 'falling away' (apostasia) and revealing of the 'man of lawlessness' (anthropos tes anomias) before the day of the Lord, and Matthew 24:14 with its global-preaching condition before 'the end' (to telos). Under this lens the no-date-setting part is affirmed without reservation ('no one knows' oudeis oiden, 'not yours to know' ouch hymon gnonai), but the strictly any-moment reading of the imminence part is qualified. The watch-commands and thief (kleptes) comparison then bear on perpetual readiness through the in-between time, not a content-free unconditional expectation.

Reads the parables of delay in the same Olivet discourse (Matthew 24:48 'delays' chronizei, Matthew 25:5 'while delaying' chronizontos) as stretching the interval, yet still affirms that the day (hemera) and hour (hora) are unknown ('no one knows' oudeis oiden) and that date-setting is excluded by 'it is not yours to know' (ouch hymon gnonai). Both the non-knowledge and the no-date-setting parts hold under this lens.

Reads the Olivet day-and-hour language as oriented in part to the first-century judgment on Jerusalem, which reduces the imminence-of-the-final-return emphasis from those verses. Even so, the word-level statements 'no one knows' (oudeis oiden) and 'it is not yours to know times or seasons' (ouch hymon gnonai chronous e kairous) still forbid presuming to know or set the time, so the no-date-setting part is unaffected.

hermeneutics.notes: The no-date-setting part is stable across every lens because the underlying word-level items (universal 'no one' oudeis with the perfect tense 'knows' oiden, a completed action whose result still stands, plus 'it is not yours to know' ouch hymon gnonai) are unambiguous. The any-moment imminence part is the one element where lenses diverge, because the canon (the whole Bible) supplies both unannounced-arrival statements and an ordered 'falling away then day' (apostasia then hemera) sequence in 2 Thessalonians 2, and the relative weight of the two is not forced by the words alone.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: The biblical texts addressing the timing of Christ's return state whether the day (hemera) and hour (hora) are humanly knowable, whether the return is presented as near and unannounced, and what posture believers are instructed to take.
stem_audit.notes: The original stem bundles three theologically loaded terms, 'imminent', 'could occur at any time', and 'date-setting is forbidden', which can preload a particular any-moment expectation that is more framework than bare word meaning. The neutralized form restates the question as what the texts say about knowability, nearness language, and the prescribed posture. The verdict was derived on the original stem, and the word-level evidence supports both the non-knowledge claim and the no-date-setting application very strongly. The any-moment phrasing of the imminence part is the one element where lenses diverge because 2 Thessalonians 2:1-3 inserts an ordered 'falling away' (apostasia) and revealing of the 'man of lawlessness' (anthropos tes anomias) 'first' (proton), before the day (hemera). Honest read: no-date-setting is decisive, generic imminence and readiness are decisive, strict any-moment imminence with no prior conditions is the contested element. The composite verdict remains true on the natural reading of the stem because the proposition does not require strict any-moment expectation, only that the return is imminent (near, possible without warning) and date-setting is forbidden. A reader who heard 'imminent' as strict any-moment would find that element more disputed, which is recorded in competing_lens_verdicts.

lay_summary: The question is whether the Bible teaches that Christ's return could happen at any time, that no one knows the exact day or hour, and that setting a date is forbidden. Reading only the Greek text and standard word-study tools, two threads run through the passages. First, knowledge of the timing is denied. Matthew 24:36 and Mark 13:32 say 'no one knows' (oudeis oiden) about the day (hemera) and hour (hora). The word 'no one' (oudeis) is a universal negative, and Mark stacks the denials so that not the angels and not even the Son know, only the Father (pater). In Acts 1:7 Jesus tells the disciples 'it is not yours to know times or seasons' (ouch hymon estin gnonai chronous e kairous), placing them in the Father's own authority. Paul echoes the same word pair, 'time' (chronos) and 'season' (kairos), in 1 Thessalonians 5:1 and says no calendar letter is needed. Second, the response commanded is watchfulness, not calculation. Matthew 24:42 uses the present imperative (ongoing command) 'keep watching' (gregoreite), grounded by 'you do not know the day'. Mark 13:33 adds 'watch, stay alert' (blepete, agrupneite), because you do not know when the time (kairos) is. The arrival is pictured as a thief in the night, 'like a thief in the night' (hos kleptes en nykti), in both Matthew 24:43 and 1 Thessalonians 5:2, an image of unannounced timing. Matthew 24:44 says be ready ('ready' hetoimoi) because the Son of Man comes at an hour you do not expect ('do not expect' ou dokeite). Philippians 4:5 says 'the Lord is near' (ho kyrios engys), James 5:8 'the coming of the Lord has drawn near' (he parousia tou kyriou engiken), and Revelation 22:20 'I come swiftly' (erchomai tachy). Together the word-level pattern is decisive that the day and hour are not humanly knowable and that fixing a date is outside the believer's province, while constant readiness is commanded. One nuance explains why readers diverge on the strength of any-moment language. 2 Thessalonians 2:1-3 inserts an ordering adverb 'first' (proton) with a 'falling away' (apostasia) and revealing of the 'man of lawlessness' (anthropos tes anomias) before the day of the Lord. The text supplies an unannounced arrival pattern and also a signs-first pattern, and the words themselves do not rank the two. So no-date-setting is settled, readiness is settled, generic nearness is settled, but strict any-moment expectation with no prior conditions is the element the canon (the whole Bible) leaves room around.
